items.text: Laws should rest on reasons that people of any religion or none can accept.
items.rationale: Public-reason liberals and secular republicans endorse; integralists and religious-law advocates reject. Ideal vs here-and-now differ where existing laws carry religious grounds.

items.text: Prayer and worship should be kept out of publicly funded schools.
items.rationale: Separationists (incl. many devout believers wary of state religion) endorse; religious conservatives reject. Concrete in any country with public or subsidised schools.

items.text: Religious organisations should be funded entirely by the voluntary gifts of their own members.
items.rationale: Strict separationists, libertarians and anarchists endorse; supporters of church taxes, faith-school funding or state churches reject. Agent-neutral; frames differ where public funding exists.

items.text: Religion and public authority should be kept strictly separate.
items.rationale: Laicite-style secularists endorse; established-church and theocratic views reject. Classic frame-split: many accept an official church here and now but not in their ideal, or vice versa.

items.text: If many citizens reject a religion's beliefs, laws based only on that religion's teachings are illegitimate.
items.rationale: Condition (religious dissent) favours Secular; consent-based secularists agree, those who hold religious truth binding regardless of assent disagree. Works in pluralist and majority-faith countries alike.

items.text: If a society's people follow many different religions or none, its public ceremonies should be free of religious content.
items.rationale: Condition (pluralism) favours Secular; secular liberals agree, those valuing civil religion or national faith traditions disagree. Pluralism is easy to picture in either frame.

items.text: If a religious rule conflicts with the general law, believers should follow the general law like everyone else.
items.rationale: One-law-for-all secularists endorse; advocates of religious exemptions or religious legal authority reject. Answerable whatever the content of the general law, so meaningful in both frames.

items.text: Religious teachings should count as a valid basis for law, like any other moral view.
items.rationale: Mirror of rel-01: Christian democrats, religious conservatives and many religious communitarians endorse; public-reason secularists reject. Frames diverge where law already draws on religion.

items.text: Religious leaders should have a formal role in making law.
items.rationale: Theocrats, integralists and supporters of clerical seats in legislatures endorse; all secularists reject. Strong but non-caricature; frames split for those under or outside such systems.

items.text: A society should have an official religion, honoured in its public ceremonies and institutions.
items.rationale: Mirror of rel-04: supporters of established churches, confessional states and religious monarchies endorse; separationists reject. Good frame-splitter in countries with or without an established faith.

items.text: Religious organisations should receive public funding for the schools, hospitals and charities they run.
items.rationale: Mirror of rel-03: Christian democrats, subsidiarity advocates and faith-school supporters endorse; strict separationists reject. Concrete policy readable in both frames.

items.text: If most people in a society share a religion, its laws should reflect that religion's moral teachings.
items.rationale: Condition (religious majority) favours Religious; religious majoritarians and traditionalists agree, secularists disagree. Shared rule makes it answerable in pluralist countries too.

items.text: If a society is losing its shared sense of right and wrong, public institutions should actively promote religion.
items.rationale: Condition (moral fragmentation) favours Religious; religious conservatives and civil-religion communitarians agree, secularists disagree. Plausible frame split: urgent here and now, moot in an ideal.

items.text: If both sides in a family dispute choose a religious court, its ruling should be enforced by law.
items.note: Religious court: a body that settles disputes using religious law.
items.rationale: Condition (mutual consent) favours Religious; supporters of religious legal pluralism agree, one-law-for-all secularists disagree. Works in both frames; keying should be checked in the blind audit since some libertarians may also agree.
